**Claude (Backend / Systems Engineer · Skeptic) — Round 2**

Codex, I read through the StoreKit walkthrough properly this time rather than just noting it's off-topic for what this phase needs, and there's an actual bug hiding in it, not just a scope mismatch. You wrote "securely store and manage user entitlements using Keychain or another secure storage mechanism" — that's exactly the kind of thing that sounds like due diligence but actually undermines the architecture this project already locked. `EntitlementGate`/`EntitlementProviding` exists specifically so there's one call site and one source of truth for entitlement state, sourced live from `Transaction.currentEntitlements` on-device, no caching layer required, because StoreKit 2 itself is the durable record — Apple keeps the receipt, not us. If you additionally cache entitlement state in Keychain, you've created a second source of truth that can drift: someone restores a purchase on a new device, or a subscription lapses while the app's been closed for a week, and now Keychain says one thing while `Transaction.currentEntitlements` says another, and whichever one the UI actually reads determines whether a real bug ships. Given `[REDACTED:high_entropy]` already says every cap-check must route through one gate reporting live status, any StoreKit implementation later has to be re-checkable against `Transaction.currentEntitlements` on every relevant transition (same `scenePhase == .active` pattern we're already using for notification permissions), not a Keychain snapshot taken once at purchase time. I'd fold that in as a concrete constraint on M7 if it's ever attempted: no persisted entitlement cache, full stop — the gate re-derives status from StoreKit each time it's asked, exactly like the notification scheduler re-derives permission status.

Second concrete catch: your milestone 1 says "configure App Store Connect with product IDs" as an executable task. There is no App Store Connect account anywhere in scope for this project — the whole brief is "runnable in the iOS Simulator via Xcode," not an App Store submission pipeline, and nothing in five phases of decisions has mentioned a developer account or real product registration. The cheatsheet you yourself pulled from says explicitly you can test locally with a `.storekit` configuration file with no sandbox account needed — that's the only version of "StoreKit setup" this project can actually execute and verify. So if M7 happens at all, its definition of done has to be "purchases/restore/entitlement-swap work correctly against a local `.storekit` file in the simulator," full stop, not "register real products in ASC," which nobody here can do or verify. Worth being explicit about that so it doesn't quietly become a blocked task nobody can close.

Beyond that, I don't think this round changed the actual plan, because nothing you wrote engages with sequencing, dependencies, or the three risks I named — this is implementation detail for one deferred, should-have milestone, not a rebuttal to the ordering of the other seven. So I'll treat the plan from round 1 as the one we're locking, with two additions: the EntitlementGate swap-test as M7's concrete acceptance criterion (if StoreKit is built, swapping `UnlimitedEntitlementProvider` for a real `StoreKitEntitlementProvider` conformer must require zero changes to any other file — that's the actual test that the abstraction paid for itself, not just "purchases work"), and the no-persisted-entitlement-cache constraint above. - **M1b / M1c — Theme.swift and the SwiftData schema (Medium, parallel, zero dependency on M1).** Theme.swift is a direct transcription of the already-locked token table. - **M5 — All-decks review scope, cross-deck queue ordering, mixed-session per-deck summary attribution (Medium).**

- **M7 — Final polish/verification pass.** `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy`, dark-mode verification across every screen, accessibility pass, run instructions.

**Verification plan:** the three-tier test strategy locked in tech_specs (`RecallCoreTests`, `RecallAppTests`, `RecallAppUITests`) maps directly onto these milestones — no tier is silently downgraded to a manual check under time pressure, and the two XCUITests get the three-consecutive-clean-runs bar specifically because of their known flakiness profile.
